work.text: He became Kuniyoshi's pupil in the autumn of 1850, but does not appear to have produced prints till some ten years later.

source.author: Laurence Binyon and J. J. O'Brien Sexton
source.title: Japanese Colour Prints

work.text: During his training, Yoshitoshi concentrated on refining his draftsmanship skills and copying his mentor's sketches. Kuniyoshi emphasized drawing from real life, which was unusual in Japanese training because the artist's goal was to communicate the essence of the subject matter rather than to furnish a literal representation of it.

moment.text: When a kabuki actor died, memorial portraits shini-e were conventionally published with his farewell poem and posthumous name.

Although his life was hard after Kuniyoshi's death in 1861, he did manage to produce some work, 44 prints of his being known from 1862. In the next two years he had sixty-three of his designs, mostly kabuki prints, published.

matters.text: He produced his first signed print when he was 14 and became an independent artist at age 20.

source.author: Art Institute of Chicago
source.title: Collection description: General Tamichi, from the series A Mirror of Famous Japanese Generals

matters.text: Kuniyoshi gave his apprentice the new artist's name "Yoshitoshi", denoting lineage in the Utagawa School. Although he was not seen as Kuniyoshi's successor during his lifetime, he is now recognized as the most important pupil of Kuniyoshi.
